In one sentence: a host with a craft or household skill has a short chat with an AI guide, and three cooperating agents turn it into a complete, free-to-host, 90-minute porch gathering, matched to neighbors who signed up to learn, with personal invitations, conversation cards and safety rules.

2.Motivation

In towns like Greenville, Texas, plenty of people live within a few minutes of each other and still go weeks without a real conversation with a neighbor. Two groups feel this most. The first is adults who carry practical knowledge nobody asks them to share: the retired seamstress who can save a torn seam, the neighbor who has changed a hundred tires, the grandmother whose biscuits are the reason people used to stop by. The second is people who want to learn those skills, or simply want company: younger adults new to town, people working from home, and anyone whose social circle has thinned out. Both groups would benefit from the same thing: a small, low-stakes reason to sit together for an afternoon.

Neighborly ties are not a nicety. Nextdoor publishes research saying that knowing as few as six neighbors reduces the likelihood of loneliness (Nextdoor). The hard part is not wanting to connect; it is the work of making it happen.

How people cope today

Today a would-be host has a handful of informal options, and each puts the work on them:

Word of mouth

Ask around at church, the library or the feed store. It works only if you already know people, and it rarely reaches the newcomer who needs it most.

Groups and flyers

Join an existing church or library group, or post a flyer. Many groups are drop-in "bring your own project" sessions with no one teaching, and flyers attract strangers with no way to screen for fit or safety.

Social apps

Post on Facebook or Nextdoor. This assumes comfort with social media, and the host still has to plan the event, handle replies, and decide who to invite.

What it costs

The cost shows up in three places. Time: planning even a short gathering means deciding on a schedule, a supply list, refreshments, how to start conversations, and who to invite, then reaching those people one by one. Effort and confidence: many natural hosts are older adults who are not comfortable with apps, and the planning burden is exactly what stops them. Loneliness: when hosting feels like too much work, it does not happen, and both the would-be teacher and the would-be learner stay home. The Front Porch Exchange tries to remove the planning and inviting work so that the only thing left for the host is the part they are good at: sharing the skill.

3.What is new here

Several good products already help people meet or share skills. The table compares the four closest alternatives with what this prototype does. Descriptions are paraphrased from the linked pages.

ProductWhat it does wellWhat is left to the userHow this app differs
Meetup Large platform for finding and running recurring hobby groups, including craft groups. The organizer plans the event and recruits members. Many craft meetups are drop-in sessions at coffee shops or libraries with no teaching (one library listing says no instruction is provided). Finding groups can take social-media know-how (Axios, 2026). Builds the whole plan for a teaching session, and the host never has to recruit: neighbors who opted in are matched and invited for them.
Nextdoor Neighborhood network with a general feed, event posts, and loneliness resources (Nextdoor). Hosting and planning are entirely up to the member; it is a general-purpose feed, not a tool built for running a gathering. Purpose-built for one kind of event: small, intergenerational, skill-sharing gatherings, with a ready-to-print kit.
Les Talents d'Alphonse (France) Connects young people who want to learn a skill with older people who want to feel useful and earn extra income. Paid, one-to-one lessons; the model is a marketplace rather than a neighborhood gathering. Small-group gatherings (2–4 guests) that cost nothing to host, aimed at connection as much as instruction.
ChatGPT used directly Can draft a schedule, a supply list or an invitation on request. No community database or matching, no guardrails, no cost tracking, and the host has to know how to prompt it. A guided interview does the prompting; deterministic tools enforce the 90 minutes, matching and safety checks; cost is measured.

Two related efforts are worth noting.1,2 Neither combines planning, matching and inviting in one tool.

What we do differently, in one list

conversational interview, one question at a time exact 90-minute schedule (checked in code) supplies that cost the host $0 matching to opted-in neighbors personal invitations sent by a volunteer coordinator conversation cards and safety rules prompt-injection, privacy and content guardrails measured cost per run

An honest caveat: Meetup, Nextdoor and Les Talents d'Alphonse are established products with real users, and this is a class prototype tested only with sample data. The contribution here is the combination: an agent pipeline that takes a non-technical host from "I can teach mending" to a printable plan with invited guests, safely and for a fraction of a cent.

1 GenConnect, a design project from the Parsons CARE Lab exploring ways to connect generations.
2 The Longest Table, community potluck events that bring neighbors together around a shared meal.

4.The agents

The app is a single Streamlit file (app.py) with three agents that run in sequence. Each has its own system prompt and function, and each hands the next one structured JSON, not the chat, which keeps context short and cheap. Deterministic Python tools do the jobs that must be exactly right: arithmetic, matching, privacy and content checks.

Agent 1 · Host Intake (planned as the "Host Intake & Story Agent")

A conversational interview that asks one short, informational question per turn, in a fixed order: first name, craft or skill, whether beginners are welcome, number of guests (2–4), location, preferred days and times, and house rules. (An earlier version also asked for a personal memory about the craft; that question was removed after testing to keep the interview practical, so the "story" part now comes from the conversation cards instead.) The prompt forbids personal questions and asking where someone lives, and uses the host's name only once. The code enforces a 12-turn cap, trims extra questions, and strips repetitive "Thank you" openers. When the agent has everything, it ends its message with the profile between ===HOST_PROFILE_START=== and ===HOST_PROFILE_END=== markers. The app hides the JSON from the chat, validates it, and starts Agents 2 and 3 automatically. If the JSON is invalid, one JSON-mode repair call is allowed.

Agent 2 · Gathering Blueprint

Receives only the HostProfile JSON and returns a Blueprint in JSON mode: a run-of-show, a supply list in which every item is owned, brought by a guest, or free (with a "no-cost swap" when something normally costs money), and a refreshment pairing. The pairing is chosen by id from a fixed catalog of four non-alcoholic Barefoot Contessa recipes, so the model cannot invent a recipe or default to water; the app fills in ingredients, a short method in our own words, an allergy note and a link to the original. Tool: validate_schedule() is an explicit Python step (not API tool-calling) that checks every segment has a title, whole-number minutes and a description, and that the minutes sum to exactly 90. Errors go back to the model for one repair pass; if that still fails, the longest segment is adjusted as a last resort, otherwise the user sees a friendly error.

Agent 3 · Community Connector & Safety

Receives the HostProfile plus a compact Blueprint summary. Its first call uses real API tool-calling: the model is forced to call match_neighbors; the app runs the matcher in Python with the trusted host profile and returns the result as a function_call_output. (If the gateway rejects the tool turn, the same tool runs as an explicit step and this is logged.) The second call writes one invitation per matched neighbor, four "Porch Story Cards", four safety rules and an optional flyer. Tool: content_guardrail_check() scans the cards, invitations and flyer for political or polarizing terms, street addresses, phone numbers and emails; if anything is flagged, the agent regenerates once, then any remaining item is replaced with a safe template.

Tools and shared services

ToolTypeWhat it does
match_neighbors()Python, offered to Agent 3 as an API functionRanks opted-in neighbors in SQLite: wanting to learn the craft scores highest (direct 50, related 25, open to anything 15), a matching skill they'd like to share scores 20, plus skill-level fit (5–15) and schedule overlap (12). An optional age-mix bonus (8) favors different generations. Indoor hosts only see neighbors who said indoors is fine. Returns up to max guests + 2 so declines leave room. The neighbors in the demo database are fictional sample data.
validate_schedule()Python, explicit stepExact 90-minute check with one repair pass.
content_guardrail_check()Python, explicit stepPolitical/polarizing keyword list plus contact-detail regexes; one regeneration, then templates.
PII sanitizer & injection detectorPython, before any model callRedacts street addresses, phone numbers and emails as [redacted]; blocks common injection phrasing without calling the model.

Which model, and why

All agents use gpt-6-luna through the course Portkey gateway, using the OpenAI Python SDK and the Responses API. It is the cheapest model available on the course key, and the outputs here are short and highly structured (a profile, a schedule, a few cards), so a small model is adequate; the deterministic tools catch the mistakes a small model is most likely to make, such as minutes that do not add up. If only an OPENAI_API_KEY is present, the app falls back to gpt-4o-mini and shows cost as "n/a (course prices apply to gpt-6-luna only)". All 52 logged calls used gpt-6-luna.

5.Tokenomics

All numbers come from runs_log.jsonl, which the app writes after every call (agent, token counts, cost, seconds and a timestamp, with no user text). The script submission/tokenomics.py reproduces every figure below. The log holds 52 calls in 10 sessions, including 7 complete pipeline runs (3 that started with a full interview and 4 that used the "Load sample host" button) and 3 interview sessions that were stopped early. The script recomputes each call's cost from its tokens; it matches the cost the app logged to within $0.000000005.

Prices (course Lecture 11, gpt-6-luna, USD per 1M tokens): input $0.10, cached input $0.01, cache write $0.125, output $0.50. Billed uncached input = input − cached − cache write. Reasoning tokens are already included in output.

Cost controls that are actually in the code

  • Cheapest course model (gpt-6-luna) for all three agents.
  • Short context for Agents 2 and 3. They never see the chat: Agent 2 gets only the profile JSON (about 685 input tokens on average), and Agent 3 gets the profile plus a compact schedule summary.
  • Prompt caching of the stable prefix. Each agent's long, stable instructions come first, marked with prompt_cache_breakpoint {"mode": "explicit"} and sent with prompt_cache_options {"mode": "explicit", "ttl": "30m"}; per-call data comes after. A sidebar toggle turns caching off, and if the gateway rejects these fields the app falls back to default caching and logs it (this never happened: all 52 calls ran in explicit mode).
  • Output caps on every call: 800 tokens for Agent 1, 2,500 for Agent 2, 400 for the tool call, 3,500 for Agent 3's write-up.
  • Interview limits: a 12-turn cap and a 1,000-character limit per message. Injection attempts are answered without calling the model at all.
  • Hard spending stop: a per-session USD budget ($0.10 default) checked before every call, plus a 60-call cap.
  • Python instead of extra model calls for matching, schedule arithmetic, recipe details and content checks.

What the logs say about caching (an honest finding)

Cached input tokens were 0 on all 52 calls. The provider did write to the cache on 17 calls (18,806 tokens) once a prompt grew past about 1,000 tokens, but no later call ever read from it. Because cache writes cost $0.125 per 1M tokens versus $0.10 for plain input, caching added about $0.00047 across the entire log of $0.014168, roughly 3%, instead of saving money.

The likely reasons, which I have not yet confirmed: (1) each agent's stable prefix is under the roughly 1,024-token minimum for a cache hit (Agent 1's first call is only about 880 tokens in total), and (2) in Agent 1 the per-turn "turn notice" sits before the growing transcript, so each new prompt diverges from the previous one early. Moving the turn counter after the transcript is a one-line change that could turn those writes into reads. We did not pad prompts to force cache hits.

Did cost cutting hurt quality?

Two kinds of evidence are available. First, the output caps were never the binding constraint: the largest outputs logged were 206 tokens for Agent 1 (cap 800), 1,595 for Agent 2 (cap 2,500) and 1,196 for Agent 3 (cap 3,500), so no output was cut short. Second, the deterministic checks never had to intervene: across all 7 pipeline runs there is no JSON repair, schedule repair, guardrail regeneration or profile-extraction call in the log, so the small model produced valid output on the first try every time. A controlled caching on/off comparison, however, was not run: every logged call had caching on.

One more caveat: two sample-host runs (39d83ad5, and Agent 2 of 67ec80eb) repeat an earlier run's token counts exactly with near-instant latency, which suggests the gateway answered from a response cache. They are counted at full price here, so the averages are, if anything, slightly high.

6.Safety

Every defense below is implemented in app.py as a plain, testable function, and each one that fires adds an entry to the session's Safety log.

RiskDefense in the codeHow we know it works
Prompt injection (chat)Host text is passed as delimited data (<<<CONVERSATION … >>>), never as instructions. detect_injection() catches "ignore previous instructions", "reveal your system prompt", role changes, jailbreak phrases and requests for API keys or .env; the app replies politely, repeats the current question, and does not call the model. Prompts tell agents never to reveal instructions or keys.Figure 8 (live block); tests "Injection detection" and "Chat: injection blocked … NO API call"
Prompt injection (database text)Database rows are untrusted too: names, skills and availability pass through neutralize_untrusted(); an unsafe name becomes "Neighbor #id"; suspicious skills are never echoed; the tool result is labeled as data.Test "Malicious DB entry … never reaches the tool result / prompt"
PII leakagesanitize_pii() redacts street addresses (including rural routes such as FM and county roads), phone numbers and emails before any model call or log write. The sign-up form rejects those details outright. runs_log.jsonl stores numbers only.Tests "PII redaction", "Chat: PII redacted before the model sees it", "Run log: … no user text"
Agent malfunctionJSON mode plus schema validators with one repair retry, then a friendly error (no loops). validate_schedule() enforces exactly 90 minutes. 12-turn cap on the interview. Network, auth and rate-limit errors are mapped to plain-English messages, never stack traces.Tests "validate_schedule", "Malfunction: invalid JSON → exactly one repair retry", "Pipeline (mocked)"
OverspendingBudgetExceeded is raised before any call once spend reaches the session budget; 60-call cap; max_output_tokens on every call; 1,000-character input cap. When the budget stops a run, the partial kit is kept.Test "Budget: BudgetExceeded raised BEFORE any API call"; Figure 7 shows the budget meter
Contentcontent_guardrail_check() flags political or polarizing terms and contact details in cards, invitations and the flyer; one regeneration, then safe templates. Off-topic requests are steered back to planning.Test "Guardrail: political card and phone number … are flagged"
Privacy and consentOnly first names and matched skills from the database ever reach prompts, the kit or logs. Adults only (age bands start at 18–34), explicit consent checkbox, opt-in flag respected, an "outdoors only" preference respected when a host is hosting indoors, and the coordinator (not the host) sends invitations.Tests "Sign-up form: rejects minors, contact details, no consent…", "match_neighbors: opted-out neighbor excluded", "Matching: indoor host skips 'outdoors only' neighbors"

Defenses working

Limitations

These safeguards are real but not airtight. PII and injection detection are regular expressions: an address written as "the blue house past the Dollar General", a phone number spelled out in words, or an injection phrased creatively can get through. The political keyword list can both miss coded language and over-flag innocent uses ("president of the garden club"). Delimiting untrusted text reduces, but does not eliminate, the chance that a model follows embedded instructions. The budget is per browser session, not per person, so a determined user could open a new session. Finally, these protections cover the software only: an in-person gathering still depends on human judgment, which is why the coordinator, not the app, sends invitations.

7.Impact

Measured: once the interview ends, the agents build a complete kit in a median of 14.0 seconds.

WhatMeasured valueSource
Kit generation (Agents 2 + 3, API time)median 14.0 s, mean 14.4 s, range 1.8–29.5 s over 7 runsruns_log.jsonl (the 1.8 s run looks like a gateway cache hit)

Model cost of one full run$0.0026Section 5
Manual planning time for the same outputsEstimate: about 2–4 hoursAuthor's estimate, not measured (breakdown below)

How the manual estimate was built (labeled as an estimate, with no outside source): drafting a timed 90-minute plan, about 30–45 minutes; working out a supply list and refreshments, 20–30 minutes; writing conversation prompts and ground rules, 15–30 minutes; finding and personally inviting three or four suitable people, 1–2 hours or more of calls, posts and follow-ups. The app replaces most of the first three and turns the fourth into a short checklist for a coordinator. Even if the true manual time were half this estimate, a two-minute interview would still be a large saving.

Real users

The app has not yet been tested with real hosts or neighbors. All runs in this report were test sessions, and every match comes from the fictional sample neighbors in the demo database.

Reach: how a coordinator could use it

The natural home for this tool is an existing community anchor, such as a public library, a church, a senior center or an extension office, with one volunteer coordinator. The coordinator collects neighbor sign-ups (on paper or on the Neighbors tab), sits with a host for a two-minute interview, prints the kit, contacts the matched neighbors using each person's stated contact preference, and ticks "Mark as invited." The host never needs a phone, an account or social media. At roughly a cent per host per month in model cost, a single coordinator's time is the real limit on reach. This is a design for deployment, not a claim of one: the app has not been deployed.

8.Limits and next steps

What does not work yet

  • Sample data only. The neighbor database is seeded with 12 fictional people; matching has never been tried on real sign-ups.
  • No real contact or scheduling workflow. The app stores a contact preference but never sends a text or email, and it does not book a date; the coordinator does that by hand.
  • Regex-based safeguards for PII, injection and political content can be bypassed (Section 6).
  • No accounts or identity checks. Anyone with the app open can add a neighbor; there is no verification or background check.
  • Adults only by design, which excludes teenagers who might be eager learners.
  • Local-only deployment. It runs from a clone on one computer with a single SQLite file; there is no hosted, multi-user version.
  • Gateway and caching caveats. Explicit cache writes never turned into reads in our logs (Section 5), and some runs appear to have been answered from a gateway response cache, which slightly distorts timing.
  • No long-term evaluation. We have not measured whether gatherings actually happen, whether people come back, or whether anyone feels less lonely.

What to build in the next month

1 · A real pilot

Partner with one library or church in Greenville; recruit 3 hosts and 15 neighbors; measure interview time, kits used and attendance.

2 · Coordinator dashboard

A private view of sign-ups, matches, invitation status and the Safety log, separate from the public site.

3 · Consented invitations

Send texts or emails only after explicit opt-in, with an easy decline link and reminders.

4 · Background checks

A partnership with the host organization for screening hosts who welcome guests indoors.

5 · Multilingual support

Spanish first, for both the interview and the printed kit.

6 · Better evaluation

A rubric for kit quality (clarity, safety, fit to the host's answers), a cache on/off cost comparison, and fixing the prompt layout so caching saves money.

The core idea has held up in testing: a short conversation plus a few well-placed Python checks is enough to turn "I could teach that" into a printed plan for an afternoon on the porch, for about a quarter of a cent. The next step is to find out whether real neighbors show up.
